correctness.rationale: For 3<=n and 1<=k<=n-2, any feasible shore has at least two selected vertices: a one-element first shore forces its matched second-shore vertex selected to dominate it, which would expose n-1>k outside neighbors. With at least two selected per shore, domination is automatic, and selected a_i has exactly n-1-|J|+1_{i in J} outside neighbors, symmetrically for selected b_j. This proves the disjoint/intersecting capacity cases necessary and sufficient. Multiplicity counts follow from elementary labelled subset choices. Minimizing these two cases yields exactly the three stated regimes and their equality classes. The comparison to K_{n,n} uses the known minimum 2(n-k). Direct adjacency-mask enumeration verifies all coefficients and minima for n<=8, and additional coefficient-level checks reach n=60; no finite test is used as an infinite proof.

value.rationale: The all-set two-shore polynomial gives every feasible cardinality and exact number of minimum configurations for a natural dense graph with one missing perfect matching. The disjoint-versus-intersecting structural split yields a sharp phase boundary: deleting the perfect matching improves the k-limited domination number by exactly two in one parameter interval, but has no effect outside it. This is stronger than an isolated exact minimum, is not determined by the known K_{n,n} value, and provides an explicit benchmark for bounded-external-load domination under structured edge failures.
